title: Functions and Program Flow
summary: Manual curation draft for the shipped UI. This parent topic keeps only compact, exam-useful material for function syntax, imports, flexible arguments, scope/return behavior, and lambda-style patterns.

main_topics.title: Functions and Imports
main_topics.summary: Defining a function, calling it correctly, and knowing which names an import statement actually creates.

must_know.title: Define with `def`, call with `()`, and return the value you want the caller to use

content.text: Use `def name(params):` to define a function. Call it with `name(...)`. `print(...)` only displays a value; `return` sends it back to the caller.
content.code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

result = add(2, 3)
print(result)  # 5

content.text: The important exam question is not what module was imported, but which name is actually available afterwards.

rows: from math import pi as constant

exam_patterns.title: Alias trap: the alias replaces the old module name in your code

rows: You must use the alias you created.
The bare name `math` was never bound.
from math import pi as constant\nconstant * r ** 2

exam_patterns.title: In multi-branch function questions, check both the logic and the exact return shape

content.text: A function can fail an exam question even when the math is almost right. Check three things: every branch assigns the needed values, the function returns the requested object shape, and helper code is used as a value rather than left as a function object.

main_topics.title: Flexible Arguments and kwargs
main_topics.summary: Reading function headers with defaults, `*args`, and `**kwargs`, and tracing what a call actually passes in.

must_know.title: Read the function header from left to right

rows: extra positional arguments as a tuple
extra keyword arguments as a dict

must_know.title: Defaults are evaluated once; never use a mutable object as the default

content.text: A list or dict default persists across calls. Use `None` and create a fresh container inside the function.

exam_patterns.title: Keyword arguments can appear in any order as long as the names match

content.text: The call order does not matter here because the argument names decide where each value goes.

exam_patterns.title: Mixed header pattern: required values first, then extras, then named options

content.text: Common exam move: `*args` collects the numbers, while a named option like `factor=` stays readable in the call.
This is compact but high-value because it combines the most common header features in one traceable example.

main_topics.title: Scope and Return Behavior
main_topics.summary: What names exist where, how values escape a function, and why `None` appears so often in function questions.

must_know.title: Scope rules to check before tracing any function

rows: Parameter names and assigned names inside a function are local by default.
They cannot be used outside that function.
If a function assigns to a name anywhere, Python treats that name as local throughout that function.
You can get `UnboundLocalError` even before the assignment line.
Use it only when you really want to change the global.
`nonlocal x` rebinds the nearest enclosing local name `x`.
Use it in nested functions when you want the inner function to update the outer function's variable.
If the caller needs a value later, return it and assign the result.
Do not expect local names to survive the call.

must_know.title: `return` sends a value back; `print` only shows it

content.text: A function that prints a value but does not return it still returns `None`. In exam traces, always ask: what comes back to the caller?

exam_patterns.title: Local-name error: computing a value inside the function does not make it global

content.code:
def power(num, factor):
    result = num ** factor
    return result

print(result)
content.text: `result` is local to `power`, so `print(result)` outside the function fails.

exam_patterns.title: Self-reference after assignment makes the name local and uninitialized

content.code:
b = 1

def main(a):
    b = b
    return a

print(main(1))
content.text: Because `b` is assigned inside `main`, Python treats it as local from the start of the function. The right-hand `b` has no value yet.

main_topics.title: Lambda and Higher-Order Patterns
main_topics.summary: Small inline functions, `map(...)`, `sorted(..., key=...)`, and the few recurring higher-order patterns that show up in exams.

rows: small inline function for one value
apply `f` to every element and materialize the result
sort by a computed comparison key

must_know.title: `map(...)` is lazy; wrap it in `list(...)` when the question expects visible values

content.text: A common wrong option prints the raw `map` object instead of materializing the mapped values.

exam_patterns.title: Sort by a property, not by the raw value

content.code:
def sort_list(x):
    return sorted(x, key=lambda num: abs(num), reverse=True)
content.text: This exact exam pattern checks whether you know that `key=` computes the comparison value and `reverse=True` flips the final order.

exam_patterns.title: Apply several functions to the same input

content.code:
funcs = [square, cube]
for i in my_list:
    results = map(lambda f: f(i), funcs)
    print(list(results))
content.text: Read `lambda f: f(i)` as: take one function from `funcs`, call it on the current number `i`, then collect the outputs.

exam_patterns.title: Check whether the function expects one number or the whole list

content.text: Many distractors fail because they pass the entire list into a function that was written for a single element. `map(f, [1,2,3])` calls `f(1)`, then `f(2)`, then `f(3)`; `f([1,2,3])` is a completely different call.
Lower-frequency than `lambda` and `map`, but still worth keeping as backup because it tests the idea that functions are objects and can be returned.
